headline_marked: [[Doom Composer]] Bobby Prince, who defined gaming soundtracks, has died
headline: Doom Composer Bobby Prince, who defined gaming soundtracks, has died
summary: Bobby Prince, the legendary composer behind the iconic soundtracks for Doom, Wolfenstein 3D, and Duke Nukem 3D, has passed away at 81. His work is preserved in the Library of Congress.
details: Robert Caskin "Bobby" Prince III, the acclaimed composer and sound designer known for his groundbreaking work in early video games, has died at the age of 81. Prince's innovative contributions helped shape the soundscape of a generation of games.

Born in 1945, Prince served in the US Army during the Vietnam War before embarking on a career in music. He became a pivotal figure in the video game industry, composing scores for landmark titles such as Doom, Doom II, Wolfenstein 3D, Rise of the Triad, and Duke Nukem 3D.

His influential music is credited with establishing video game scores as a respected art form. In recognition of his achievements, Prince received a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2006. The soundtrack for the original Doom was selected for preservation in the Library of Congress in 2026, cementing his legacy.

Beyond his professional achievements, Prince was remembered for his kindness, humor, and deep love for his family. He shared 21 years of marriage with his wife, Connie Freeman Prince, with whom he collaborated on various creative projects.

headline_marked: [[Chefs of brutal leaders]] from Idi Amin to Saddam Hussein talk about their unusual lives
headline: Chefs of brutal leaders from Idi Amin to Saddam Hussein talk about their unusual lives
summary: A new documentary, 'How to Feed a Dictator,' features five private chefs recounting their intimate experiences serving some of the world's most feared dictators, revealing the extraordinary stakes and moral dilemmas of their jobs.
details: The new documentary 'How to Feed a Dictator,' premiering at the Tribeca film festival, features five private chefs who served notorious strongmen like Idi Amin and Saddam Hussein. It delves into their intimate experiences, revealing how the dining table became a stage for power and every meal carried extraordinary stakes.

The film, based on Witold Szabłowski's 2020 book, probes the fraught terrain between morality and survival. It asks viewers to consider the choices these chefs made, often under duress, and how beloved everyday things like food took on a different dimension within a dictatorship.

Perspectives vary widely, from Keo Samoun, who still regards Pol Pot almost as a god, to Ermanno Furlanis, who recalls the terror of making pizzas for Kim Jong-il. Furlanis's life was under surveillance, his passport guarded, and even the spacing of olives on a pizza was meticulously controlled by state apparatchiks.

Ugandan chef Charles Otonde Odera, who served Idi Amin, describes his early days as life-changing, going from a poor villager to driving a Mercedes and supporting eight wives. This comfort came at the cost of serving a brutal regime, a trade-off many chefs made, as one director noted: 'It was just business.'

Odera began to reconsider his bargain after Amin's second wife was found dead amid rumors of her murder. He recounts being ordered to cook a human heart, with Amin claiming it prevented haunting. Odera also faced a death sentence after one of Amin's children suffered a stomach ache from a meal.

The film implicitly addresses why chefs didn't poison dictators, suggesting deep trust was required to enter their inner circle, which also ensured distance from such thoughts. Interestingly, Saddam Hussein's love for masgouf, a grilled carp dish, ultimately helped US forces locate him after his regime fell.
